notes:
Mole concept

  • 1 mole $= 6.022\times10^{23}$ particles $=$ molar mass in grams $= 22.4$ L of any gas at STP (0 °C, 1 atm) [22.7 L at 1 bar].
  • Moles $= \dfrac{\text{mass}}{\text{molar mass}} = \dfrac{\text{volume at STP}}{22.4} = \dfrac{\text{no. of particles}}{N_A}$.
  • Mass of one atom $= \dfrac{\text{atomic mass}}{N_A}$ g.

Laws of chemical combination

  • Conservation of mass (Lavoisier); definite proportions (Proust); multiple proportions (Dalton: CO and CO$_2$); Gay-Lussac (gaseous volumes); Avogadro (equal volumes → equal molecules at same $T, P$).

Formulae

  • Empirical formula: simplest whole-number ratio; molecular formula $= n\times$ empirical, $n = \dfrac{\text{molar mass}}{\text{empirical formula mass}}$.
  • Percentage composition $= \dfrac{\text{mass of element}}{\text{molar mass}}\times100$.

Concentration terms

Molarity $M$mol solute / L solution (depends on $T$)
Molality $m$mol solute / kg solvent (independent of $T$)
Mole fraction $x$$n_A/(n_A+n_B)$; $\sum x = 1$
Mass %mass solute / mass solution × 100
Dilution$M_1V_1 = M_2V_2$

Limiting reagent

The reactant that is completely consumed first; it decides the amount of product. Convert all masses to moles and compare with the stoichiometric ratio.

Exam tip

Two questions typically: 'which contains maximum atoms/molecules' and a molarity/limiting-reagent numerical. Memorise molar masses: H$_2$O 18, CO$_2$ 44, NaOH 40, H$_2$SO$_4$ 98, CaCO$_3$ 100, NaCl 58.5, glucose 180, urea 60.

questions.q: The number of moles in 8.8 g of CO$_2$ is
questions.explanation: Molar mass of CO$_2 = 44$ g mol$^{-1}$; $8.8/44 = 0.2$ mol.
questions.trick: Moles = mass ÷ molar mass; no need to find molecules first.

questions.q: The number of molecules in 4.4 g of CO$_2$ is
questions.trick: Find moles first, then × $N_A$; never multiply mass by $N_A$ directly.

questions.q: A compound contains 40% C, 6.67% H and 53.33% O by mass. Its empirical formula is
questions.trick: Divide %s by atomic mass, then divide all by the smallest for the ratio.

questions.q: 4 g of H$_2$ reacts with 16 g of O$_2$ to form water. The mass of water formed is
questions.explanation: $2\text{H}_2 + \text{O}_2 \to 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$. H$_2$: 2 mol, O$_2$: 0.5 mol. O$_2$ is limiting; 0.5 mol O$_2$ gives 1 mol H$_2$O = 18 g.
questions.tip: Always find the limiting reagent first.
questions.trick: Convert to moles and compare with stoichiometric ratio, not raw mass.

questions.q: 4 g of NaOH is dissolved in water to make 250 mL of solution. The molarity is
questions.trick: $M$ = moles ÷ litres of solution, not of solvent.

questions.q: Which concentration term is independent of temperature?
questions.explanation: Molality uses mass of solvent, which does not change with temperature; molarity uses volume, which does.
questions.trick: Mass-based terms (molality) don't shift with $T$; volume-based ones do.

questions.q: The volume occupied by 0.5 mol of any gas at STP (0 °C, 1 atm) is
questions.explanation: 1 mol occupies 22.4 L at STP, so 0.5 mol → 11.2 L.
questions.trick: 1 mol = 22.4 L at STP; just scale linearly by moles.

questions.q: Carbon forms two oxides CO and CO$_2$. This illustrates the law of
questions.explanation: Masses of O combining with a fixed mass of C (12 g) are 16 and 32, in a simple ratio 1:2 — Dalton's law of multiple proportions.
questions.trick: Same C, O masses in a simple whole-number ratio → multiple proportions.

questions.q: Which of the following contains the largest number of atoms?
questions.explanation: H$_2$: $\tfrac12$ mol molecules $= 1$ mol atoms. He: 0.25 mol atoms. O$_2$: $\tfrac1{32}\times2 = 0.0625$ mol. CH$_4$: $\tfrac1{16}\times5 = 0.3125$ mol. Hydrogen wins.
questions.trick: Divide 1 g by molar mass, × atoms/molecule; lightest atom per molecule wins.

questions.q: The mole fraction of ethanol in a solution containing 46 g ethanol and 18 g water is
questions.trick: $x$ = mol of component ÷ total mol, never mass ÷ total mass.

questions.q: The mass of one atom of carbon-12 is approximately
questions.trick: Atomic mass ÷ $N_A$ gives the mass of one atom in grams.

questions.q: The volume of 0.5 M H$_2$SO$_4$ required to prepare 500 mL of 0.1 M solution is
questions.explanation: $M_1V_1 = M_2V_2 \Rightarrow V_1 = 0.1\times500/0.5 = 100$ mL.
questions.trick: $M_1V_1 = M_2V_2$; plug in and solve for the unknown volume.

questions.q: The molality of a solution containing 5 g of NaOH in 200 g of water is
questions.trick: $m$ = moles solute ÷ kg solvent, never kg of solution.

questions.q: Percentage of oxygen by mass in H$_2$SO$_4$ is approximately
questions.explanation: Molar mass 98; O $= 64$; $64/98\times100 \approx 65.3\%$.
questions.trick: % element = (mass of element ÷ molar mass) × 100.

questions.q: Equal volumes of all gases under the same conditions of temperature and pressure contain equal numbers of molecules. This is
questions.explanation: Avogadro's hypothesis (1811), which explained Gay-Lussac's law of gaseous volumes.
questions.trick: Equal volumes, equal molecules, same $T,P$ → Avogadro's law, by definition.

questions.q: The number of atoms present in 0.5 mol of N$_2$ gas is
questions.explanation: 0.5 mol N$_2$ = 1 mol N atoms = $6.022\times10^{23}$ atoms.
questions.trick: Atoms = moles × atomicity × $N_A$; N$_2$ is diatomic.

questions.q: The vapour density of a gas is 22. Its molecular mass is
questions.explanation: Molecular mass $= 2\times$ vapour density $= 2\times22 = 44$.
questions.trick: Molecular mass = 2 × vapour density, always — pure recall.

questions.q: 5.6 L of a gas at STP weighs 11 g. Its molar mass is
questions.trick: Moles = $V/22.4$ at STP, then molar mass = mass ÷ moles.

questions.q: The law of reciprocal proportions is illustrated by the combination of C, H and O in which set of compounds?
questions.explanation: When H and O each combine separately with a fixed mass of C (as in CH$_4$ and CO$_2$), the ratio of their masses equals the ratio in which they combine directly (as in H$_2$O) — the law of reciprocal proportions.
questions.trick: Two elements combining separately with a third matching their direct-combination ratio → reciprocal proportions.

questions.q: 3.2 g of CH$_4$ is mixed with 3.2 g of O$_2$ and reacted as CH$_4 + 2\text{O}_2 \to \text{CO}_2 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$. The mass of CO$_2$ formed is
questions.explanation: Moles: CH$_4 = 0.2$, O$_2 = 0.1$. O$_2$ needs $0.05$ mol CH$_4$ only, so O$_2$ is limiting. CO$_2$ formed $= 0.1/2 = 0.05$ mol $= 2.2$ g.
questions.tip: Compare mol ratio available to mol ratio required, not just masses.
questions.trick: Compare moles needed vs moles available from the equation, not raw masses.

questions.q: The number of significant figures in 0.00620 is
questions.explanation: Leading zeros are not significant; 6, 2 and the trailing 0 are significant, giving 3 significant figures.
questions.trick: Leading zeros never count; only 6, 2 and the trailing 0 are significant.

questions.q: Which of the following numbers has exactly three significant figures?
questions.explanation: 2.50 has three significant figures (2, 5, 0); leading zeros in 0.025 and 0.0025 are not significant.
questions.trick: A trailing zero after the decimal point counts as significant.

questions.q: A hydrated salt CuSO$_4\cdot x\text{H}_2\text{O}$ contains 36% water by mass. The value of $x$ is (Cu = 64, S = 32)
questions.explanation: Molar mass of CuSO$_4 = 160$. $\dfrac{18x}{160+18x} = 0.36 \Rightarrow 18x = 57.6+6.48x \Rightarrow x = 5$, matching CuSO$_4\cdot5\text{H}_2\text{O}$.
questions.trick: Set water's mass fraction $= 18x/(M+18x)$ and solve for $x$.

questions.q: 4 g of a divalent metal reacts completely with excess acid to liberate 2.24 L of H$_2$ at STP. The atomic mass of the metal is
questions.explanation: Moles H$_2 = 0.1$; equivalents $= 0.2$ (1 mol H$_2$ = 2 eq). Equivalent mass of metal $= 4/0.2 = 20$; atomic mass $=$ equivalent mass $\times$ valency $= 20\times2 = 40$.
questions.trick: Equivalent mass = mass ÷ equivalents; atomic mass = eq. mass × valency.

questions.q: In a reaction, the theoretical yield of a product is 20 g but only 15 g is actually obtained. The percentage yield is
questions.trick: % yield = (actual ÷ theoretical) × 100 — direct plug-in.

questions.q: 200 mL of 0.5 M HCl is mixed with 300 mL of 0.2 M HCl. The molarity of the resulting solution is
questions.trick: Total moles ÷ total volume; moles simply add, volumes simply add.

questions.q: 1 ppm (mass/mass) of a solute in solution is equivalent to
questions.explanation: Parts per million by mass means 1 part solute in $10^6$ parts solution, i.e. 1 mg solute per kg of solution.
questions.trick: ppm (mass/mass) = mg solute per kg solution — memorise the unit.

questions.q: The empirical formula of a compound is CH$_2$O and its empirical formula mass is 30. If its molar mass is 180, the molecular formula is
questions.explanation: $n = 180/30 = 6$; molecular formula $= 6\times$CH$_2$O $=$ C$_6$H$_{12}$O$_6$ (glucose).
questions.trick: $n$ = molar mass ÷ empirical mass; multiply the empirical formula by $n$.

questions.q: A sample of impure CaCO$_3$ (80% pure) weighing 12.5 g is heated completely as $\text{CaCO}_3 \to \text{CaO} + \text{CO}_2$. The mass of CO$_2$ released is (Ca = 40)
questions.explanation: Pure CaCO$_3 = 0.80\times12.5 = 10$ g $= 0.1$ mol, giving $0.1$ mol CO$_2 = 4.4$ g.
questions.trick: Use only the pure fraction (purity% × mass) before converting to moles.

questions.q: The molecular mass of Ca(OH)$_2$ is (Ca = 40, O = 16, H = 1)
questions.trick: Add up atomic masses per formula unit directly, no shortcuts needed.

questions.q: $3.011\times10^{23}$ molecules of CO$_2$ have a mass of
questions.trick: Molecules ÷ $N_A$ = moles; moles × molar mass = mass.

questions.q: 1 g each of CH$_4$, CO$_2$, H$_2$O(g) and N$_2$ is taken. The correct order of increasing number of moles is
questions.explanation: Moles per gram $= 1/M$: CO$_2$ (1/44=0.023) < N$_2$ (1/28=0.036) < H$_2$O (1/18=0.056) < CH$_4$ (1/16=0.063). Lower molar mass gives more moles for the same mass.
questions.trick: Moles per gram $= 1/M$; the smaller the molar mass, the more moles.

questions.q: Which of the following statements is INCORRECT?
options: Molarity is expressed in mol per kg of solvent
Molality does not change with temperature
1 mole of any gas occupies 22.4 L at STP
questions.explanation: Molarity is moles of solute per litre of solution, not per kg of solvent — that is the definition of molality.
questions.trick: Molarity is always per litre of solution, never per kg of solvent.

questions.q: A mixture contains 4.4 g of CO$_2$ and 2.8 g of N$_2$. The total number of molecules present in the mixture is
questions.trick: Find moles of each species separately, add them, then × $N_A$.

questions.q: Pure water samples obtained from a river, a well and a laboratory synthesis all contain hydrogen and oxygen in the mass ratio 1:8. This observation illustrates the
questions.explanation: A pure compound always contains its constituent elements in a fixed mass ratio regardless of source — the law of definite (constant) proportions.
questions.trick: Same ratio regardless of source → law of definite proportions.

questions.q: On complete combustion, 0.6 g of an organic compound (containing C, H and O only) gives 0.88 g CO$_2$ and 0.36 g H$_2$O. The empirical formula of the compound is
questions.tip: Any mass not accounted for by C and H in a combustion problem is oxygen.
questions.trick: Mass left over after accounting for C and H is oxygen.

questions.q: What volume of water must be added to 100 mL of 0.5 M HCl to make it 0.1 M?
questions.explanation: $M_1V_1 = M_2V_2 \Rightarrow 0.5\times100 = 0.1\times V_2 \Rightarrow V_2 = 500$ mL. Water to be added $= 500-100 = 400$ mL.
questions.trick: Find final volume via $M_1V_1=M_2V_2$, then subtract the initial volume.

questions.q: The SI unit of the amount of a substance is the
questions.explanation: The mole is the SI base unit for amount of substance.
questions.trick: Mole is the SI base unit for amount of substance — direct recall.

questions.q: The normality of a solution containing 4.9 g of H$_2$SO$_4$ in 500 mL of solution is (H = 1, S = 32, O = 16)
questions.explanation: Equivalent mass of H$_2$SO$_4 = 98/2 = 49$; equivalents $= 4.9/49 = 0.1$; normality $= 0.1/0.5 = 0.2$ N.
questions.trick: $N$ = equivalents ÷ litres; eq. mass of H$_2$SO$_4$ = molar mass/2.

questions.q: 5.4 g of Al reacts with 4.48 L of Cl$_2$ at STP as $2\text{Al} + 3\text{Cl}_2 \to 2\text{AlCl}_3$. The mass of Al left unreacted is (Al = 27)
questions.explanation: Moles: Al $= 0.2$, Cl$_2 = 4.48/22.4 = 0.2$. Cl$_2$ needs $0.2\times2/3 = 0.1333$ mol Al to react fully, so Cl$_2$ is limiting. Unreacted Al $= 0.2-0.1333 = 0.0667$ mol $= 1.8$ g.
questions.trick: Find limiting reagent by mole ratio needed; only excess reactant remains unreacted.
